summary.name: Monitoring Isn't Observability
summary.one_liner: A 2017 essay by Baron Schwartz arguing that observability is a property of a system, distinct from monitoring, tools, and debugging, and that the term is often misused as a buzzword.
keywords: monitoring tells you whether system works
use_cases: Clarifying the difference between monitoring and observability
Evaluating whether a vendor's observability claims are meaningful
Building an observability culture in an engineering team
summary.what_it_does: The essay defines observability as a system attribute, using the control-theory definition from Wikipedia and an analogy: observability is the clarity of the slide under the microscope, not the microscope itself. It separates observability from related terms such as instrumentation, telemetry, analytics, and monitoring, noting that monitoring is a verb while observability is a noun. It also describes observability as a cultural trait, with observability teams working to close the loop between data and action. Finally, it argues that writers often use "observability" where "tools", "monitoring", or "debugging" would be clearer, and it closes with the summary that monitoring tells you whether a system works while observability lets you ask why it isn't.
notable: Summarizes the idea as: monitoring tells you whether a system works; observability lets you ask why it isn't
Microscope/slide analogy for observability versus tooling
Argues observability is a cultural value, and that tools alone achieve nothing
Written by Baron Schwartz, author of Best Practices for Architecting Highly Monitorable Applications
caveats: This is an opinion essay, not a product, so it has no pricing or platform details
The page is from 2017 and predates much of the current observability tooling landscape
